p2_8b_general_description: The SimMan Critical Care is a tetherless, full-body patient simulator built for high-fidelity training in respiratory care, anesthesia, critical care, and emergency medicine. It integrates onboard ASL 5000 lung technology so learners can connect any real mechanical ventilator in any mode and move the patient seamlessly from pre-hospital care to the ICU.  Each SimMan Critical Care system comes complete with the full-body adult manikin—configured with either articulating NIBP arms or RFID medication-recognition arms alongside LiveShock or defibrillation studs—and two pre-installed rechargeable Lithium-ion batteries for tetherless operation. To run scenarios and connect monitoring equipment, the package includes a Wi-Fi dongle, the LLEAP (Laerdal Learning Application) software and license, and a set of simulated patient cables. It also ships with a wounds kit for trauma moulage, specially designed clothing (shirt and trousers), and two wheeled transport trolley bags sized separately for the torso and legs.
p2_8c_essential_characteristics: The item is a full-body, tetherless adult patient simulator designed for high-fidelity medical training in critical care, respiratory therapy, anesthesia, and emergency medicine. It must replicate human anatomy and physiology to allow healthcare learners to practice airway management, mechanical ventilation, resuscitation, trauma care, and clinical decision-making using standard medical equipment, transitioning seamlessly from pre-hospital transport to an intensive care setting. The simulator must feature an integrated high-fidelity lung simulation system capable of interfacing directly with standard clinical mechanical ventilators across volume, pressure, and spontaneous breathing modes, maintaining positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) at any clinical level while allowing independent adjustment of left and right lung compliance and airway resistance, and supporting bag-valve-mask ventilation, non-invasive ventilation, anesthesia delivery, and ventilator weaning scenarios. Its airway must accommodate oral and nasal intubation, supraglottic airway devices, and surgical cricothyrotomy, with the ability for instructors to dynamically simulate complications such as tongue swelling, laryngospasm, pharyngeal swelling, and jaw clenching (trismus). For cardiovascular and resuscitation training, the system must output 12-lead ECG signals, support 4-wire cardiac monitoring, pacing, cardioversion, and live defibrillation (via direct pads or training studs), generate palpable pulses (carotid, femoral, radial, brachial, and pedal) that automatically adjust to simulated blood pressure, and provide realistic chest resistance that tracks compression depth, release, and rate in real time according to standard resuscitation guidelines. Additionally, the manikin must simulate arterial and venous bleeding, fluid secretions (sweat, tears, saliva, blood), blinking and light-reactive pupils, and urinary catheterization, while offering limb configurations that support either realistic joint articulation with non-invasive blood pressure (NIBP) cuff readings or automated medication recognition via radio-frequency identification (RFID).
p2_8_5_mounting: The system requires no permanent structural mounting, seismic anchoring, bulkhead fastening, or overhead suspension.
p2_8_7_unique_reqs: The system requires no dedicated facility utility hookups—such as hardwired electrical circuits, piped medical gases, compressed air lines, or plumbing/drainage connections. All utility needs are met through standard room infrastructure and self-contained internal systems
p2_8_9_support_desc: The capability of the manufacturer to provide certified, on-site local maintenance, preventive servicing, and rapid technical support is critical to operational readiness. Unlike basic task trainers, a high-fidelity critical care simulator integrates complex electro-mechanical lung mechanics, precision pneumatic valves, fluid reservoirs, pulse actuators, internal power systems, and wireless telemetry that local staff cannot repair without proprietary diagnostic tools and factory-certified parts. Relying on depot-level shipping ("return-to-bench" repair) for a full-body manikin weighing approximately 85 to 88 pounds creates multi-week turnaround delays, directly disrupting scheduled clinical rotations, residency training, and critical care courses. Furthermore, because the system depends on wireless communication and scenario-control software to interface with bedside monitors and debriefing equipment, on-site field service engineers and technical specialists are essential for resolving network configuration conflicts, executing firmware updates, performing annual calibrations, and preserving original manufacturer warranty coverage without risking costly downtime.
p2_8_10_training_explain:
formal operator training is required to safely operate, maintain, and integrate the simulator into clinical training curricula.

Formal manufacturer-led operator training is essential because a high-fidelity critical care simulator requires specialized technical proficiency beyond basic manikin handling. Operators and simulation technicians must be trained to properly configure wireless network telemetry, operate scenario-control software, program real-time physiological trends, and adjust complex internal lung mechanics—such as left/right lung compliance, airway resistance, and positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP)—to interface safely with live clinical mechanical ventilators. Additionally, improper fluid management, incorrect battery charging protocols, or the misuse of supplemental oxygen and live defibrillation equipment can cause severe internal damage to pneumatic valves and electronic circuitry or create safety hazards for staff and learners. Structured initial training ensures simulation personnel can execute pre-scenario system checks, manage consumable replacements, perform routine post-use purging and cleaning, and troubleshoot software or hardware faults independently, maximizing system reliability and protecting the capital investment.
p3_9a_current_function: Currently, the center accomplishes this training function using an aging high-fidelity patient simulator that serves as the primary workhorse for critical care, respiratory therapy, anesthesia, and emergency medicine simulations. However, the existing unit has reached the end of its serviceable lifecycle, experiencing degraded internal electro-mechanical components, intermittent telemetry failures, and declining reliability that disrupt scheduled training exercises. While the center maintains other patient simulators in its inventory, those assets cannot absorb this workload because they lack the specialized high-fidelity lung mechanics required to interface with real clinical mechanical ventilators, or they are fully committed to other concurrent training programs under existing fleet rotation schedules. Consequently, this acquisition is a direct lifecycle replacement required to retire a no-longer-functional unit and restore uninterrupted, high-acuity clinical simulation capacity without displacing other active curricula.
p3_9b_staffing_info: The Department of Simulation currently operates with 21 personnel across clinical, technical, operational, and administrative specialties. Of that workforce, 14 staff members directly operate, program, maintain, or facilitate clinical instruction using the high-fidelity critical care simulator, while the remaining 7 personnel provide essential scheduling, logistics, standardized patient, and administrative support.
p3_9c_conjunction_explain: Yes, the patient simulator is designed to operate fully integrated with a wide range of existing medical, clinical, and simulation equipment within the facility. In daily operations, it will interface directly with real clinical mechanical ventilators across volume, pressure, and spontaneous breathing modes to simulate complex pulmonary mechanics, positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) management, and ventilation weaning scenarios. It will also connect with dedicated simulated bedside monitors and facility telemetry systems to display real-time physiological parameters, including 12-lead ECG waveforms, oxygen saturation, non-invasive blood pressure, and invasive hemodynamic pressures. For resuscitation and emergency care exercises, learners will use standard clinical defibrillators, cardiac pacemakers, and automated external defibrillators (AEDs) via training adapters or direct pads for live rhythm interpretation, cardioversion, and defibrillation. Furthermore, the system will integrate with the center's existing audiovisual recording, camera tracking, and debriefing software to capture learner performance, vital-sign overlays, and event logs for structured post-scenario reviews. Finally, the manikin will be used alongside standard clinical airway instruments (such as laryngoscopes, endotracheal tubes, supraglottic airways, and cricothyrotomy kits), vascular access supplies, point-of-care diagnostic ultrasound units, and standard hospital beds, stretchers, and crash carts to support seamless patient movement across emergency and intensive care environments.
